children.note: How to find the law in Kenya, read and cite it, and write clear answers, memos and essays. These are the working skills behind every other law course. A study aid for review, not legal advice.

nodeData.note: How to find the law in Kenya, read and cite it, and write clear answers, memos and essays. These are the working skills behind every other law course. A study aid for review, not legal advice.

children.note: Legal research means finding the rules that answer a question, and checking they are still good law. Start with the big picture, then narrow down to the exact rule.
A lawyer's advice is only as good as the law behind it. Clients, courts and examiners all expect you to show where each rule comes from.
The law itself: the Constitution, Acts of Parliament, rules made under Acts, and court decisions. These are what you rely on in an answer.

manas.q: What is a primary source of law?

children.note: Books, journal articles, commentaries and study notes that explain the law. They help you understand and find the law, but they are not the law.

manas.q: What is a secondary source, and can you rely on it as the law?

children.note: A binding authority must be followed by a court (for example, a decision of a higher Kenyan court). A persuasive one, like an English or other Commonwealth case, may guide the court but need not be followed.

manas.q: What is the difference between binding and persuasive authority?

children.note: A good habit: read a textbook chapter to learn the topic and get leads, then go to the actual Acts and cases and cite those.
The Constitution of Kenya 2010 is the highest law. Any Act or rule that conflicts with it is invalid, so check it first on any public-law question.
Statutes passed by Parliament, such as the Penal Code or the Law of Contract Act. Always use the latest version, because Acts are amended often.
Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org), run by the National Council for Law Reporting, publishes court decisions and the laws of Kenya online for free. It is the first stop for Kenyan cases.

manas.q: Where would you first look for a Kenyan court decision online?

children.note: University libraries often subscribe to paid databases with foreign cases and journals. Ask your law library which ones your student login covers.
The government's official weekly publication. New laws, legal notices and official appointments are announced there, so it shows when something took effect.

manas.q: What is the Kenya Gazette used for in legal research?

children.note: Your faculty library and court libraries hold printed law reports, older statutes and textbooks that may not be online. Librarians are expert guides, so ask them.
Before relying on a case, check that a higher court has not overruled it. Before relying on an Act, check it has not been amended or repealed.

manas.q: What two things should you check before relying on a case or an Act?

children.note: A judgment can be long. A case brief is your one-page summary of what matters, so you can revise and use the case quickly.
Many reports start with a short summary written by the editor. It helps you find your way, but it is not part of the judgment, so never quote it as the court's words.
What happened between the parties, in a few lines. Keep only the facts the court needed to decide the case.

manas.q: In a case brief, what goes under 'Facts'?

children.note: The legal question the court had to answer, ideally written as one question that can be answered yes or no.

manas.q: What is the 'issue' in a case brief?

children.note: The court's answer to the issue and the outcome, for example 'appeal dismissed' or 'the claim succeeds'.

manas.q: What is the 'holding' of a case?

children.note: Why the court decided as it did: the rules it applied and how it applied them. This is the most useful part for later problem questions.
The ratio is the legal principle needed for the decision, and it is what binds later courts. Obiter remarks are side comments, which are only persuasive.

manas.q: What is the difference between ratio decidendi and obiter dicta?

children.note: A judge who disagrees writes a dissent. It is not law, but it shows the counter-argument and sometimes becomes the law later.

House of Lords, 1932. Facts: a woman fell ill after drinking ginger beer with a snail in it. Issue: does a maker owe a duty to the final consumer without a contract? Holding: yes, 3–2. Reasoning: Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle'.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
A citation tells the reader exactly where to find your source. Accurate citations make your work trustworthy and let a marker check it.
To show the authority for each point, to let others check it, and to give credit to other writers. Uncited claims carry little weight.
Usually: party names joined by 'v', the year, the report series, the volume and the first page. A neutral citation identifies the court and the judgment number instead of a printed report.

manas.q: What are the usual parts of a case citation?

children.note: In a civil case, 'Smith v Jones' is read aloud as 'Smith and Jones', not 'versus'. In English criminal cases 'R' stands for the Crown (Rex or Regina).
Point to the exact page or paragraph you rely on, not just the whole judgment. This saves the reader time and shows you read the case closely.

manas.q: What is a pinpoint citation?

children.note: Give the full short title of the Act and the section you rely on. Say which version or amendment you mean if it has changed recently.
Kenyan writers mostly follow English-style citation. Kenya Law shows a citation for each judgment it publishes; follow your faculty's style guide on exactly how to set it out.
OSCOLA (Oxford University Standard for Citation of Legal Authorities) is a UK style guide used by many law schools. Some Kenyan teachers use it; check what your course requires.
Pick one style and use it the same way throughout. Mixed styles look careless and cost marks.
Footnotes cite the source at the point you use it. A bibliography or table of authorities lists all cases, statutes and books at the end.
A problem question gives a story and asks what the law says. IRAC and CREAC are simple frames to organise a clear answer.
Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. Spot the legal question, state the law, apply it to these facts, then give your answer.

manas.q: What does IRAC stand for?

children.note: Find each legal problem hidden in the story. Most exam questions have several issues; deal with them one at a time.
Give the rule with its authority: the Act and section, or the case that set it. Keep it short and accurate.
Link the rule to the specific facts. Say why each fact helps or hurts each side. This is where most marks are won or lost.

manas.q: In IRAC, which step usually earns the most marks?

children.note: Say what the likely outcome is, and how sure you are. It is fine to say 'probably', as long as you explain why.
Conclusion, Rule, Explanation, Application, Conclusion. You state the answer at the start, explain how courts have used the rule, then apply it and repeat the answer.

manas.q: What does CREAC stand for, and how is it different from IRAC?

children.note: IRAC suits most exam answers. CREAC suits memos and essays where the reader wants the answer up front.
Wanjiku rides a matatu in Nairobi. The driver speeds through a pothole and she breaks her wrist. Does she have a claim against the driver? (A study example, not legal advice.)
Did the driver owe Wanjiku a duty of care, and did he breach it by speeding so that she was hurt?
Negligence needs a duty of care, a breach of it, and harm caused by the breach. Donoghue v Stevenson's neighbour principle shapes the duty, and Kenyan courts treat it as persuasive.

A driver can clearly foresee that careless driving will hurt passengers, so a duty exists. Speeding into a pothole falls below a careful driver's standard. Her broken wrist came straight from that jolt.
Wanjiku probably has a good claim in negligence. A full answer would also check Kenyan cases and any defence, such as the owner's insurance or her own carelessness.
Good answers show what each party would say before reaching a view. Examiners reward balance, not just the 'right' answer.

children.topic: Writing memos, essays and plain English
children.note: Legal writing must be clear, accurate and easy to follow. The reader is busy, so get to the point.
A memo is an internal note answering a legal question for a senior lawyer or client file. It is objective: it shows the weak points as well as the strong ones.

manas.q: What is a legal memo, and should it be one-sided?

children.note: A common order: heading, question presented, short answer, facts, discussion and conclusion. Put the short answer near the top.
State the exact question in one sentence, then answer it in two or three. A reader who stops there should still know the result.
Work through each issue using IRAC or CREAC, with authorities. Use headings so the reader can find each issue fast.
An essay asks you to discuss or argue about the law, not to solve a story. You need a clear thesis (your main argument) and evidence for it.

manas.q: How does a legal essay differ from a problem question?

children.note: Introduction with your thesis and roadmap; body paragraphs, each making one point with authority; conclusion that answers the question set.
Do not just describe the law. Say whether it works well, who it helps or harms, and how it could change, with reasons.
Write short sentences in everyday words. Use a legal term when it is needed, and explain it the first time.

manas.q: What is the main rule of plain legal English?

children.note: Replace 'hereinafter' and 'the said' with simple words. Avoid Latin phrases unless they are standard terms, such as ratio decidendi.
'The court dismissed the appeal' is clearer than 'the appeal was dismissed by the court'. Active voice shows who did what.
Leave time to reread. Check names, dates, section numbers and citations; small errors make the whole piece look unreliable.
Your work must be your own, and every source must be real and checked. Honesty is a core duty of a lawyer.
Passing off someone else's words or ideas as your own, even by accident. Copying a textbook, a classmate or a website without credit all count.

manas.q: What is plagiarism?

children.note: Use quotation marks for exact words. When you paraphrase, rewrite fully in your own words. Cite the source in both cases.
Universities treat plagiarism as serious misconduct; it can mean failing a paper or worse. For a future advocate, a record of dishonesty can harm admission.
Some materials are protected by copyright under Kenya's Copyright Act. Short quotations with credit for study are normal; copying whole works is not.
AI chatbots can explain a topic, suggest search terms or tidy your grammar. Treat them like a quick tutor, not a source of law.
AI tools sometimes make up cases, quotes and citations that look real. These are called 'hallucinations'.

manas.q: What is an AI 'hallucination' in legal research?

children.topic: A real warning: Mata v Avianca
children.note: In this 2023 US federal case, lawyers filed a brief with fake cases made up by ChatGPT. The judge fined them US$5,000.
Open each case and section yourself on Kenya Law or in the library. If you cannot find it, do not use it.

manas.q: What must you do with every citation an AI tool gives you?

children.note: Check your faculty's policy on AI use, and say when you used it if asked. Never paste confidential client facts into a public AI tool.
Law exams test clear thinking under time pressure. Plan your time and avoid the classic mistakes.
Divide the time by the marks each question carries, and stick to it. A half-answer to every question beats a perfect answer to one.

manas.q: How should you split your time in a law exam?

children.note: Read the question twice and underline the key facts. Spend a few minutes listing issues before you write.
Read the instruction words ('advise X', 'discuss', 'critically evaluate'). Advising only one party when asked about both loses marks.
Long rule-dumps with no link to the facts score poorly. Apply the law to the story.
A rule with no case or section behind it looks like opinion. Name your authority, even briefly.

children.topic: Trap: English law for Kenyan law
children.note: English cases are often persuasive only. Where a Kenyan Act or the Constitution covers the point, start with that.

manas.q: Why should you not rely on English cases alone in a Kenyan law exam?

children.note: Keep five minutes at the end to reread for missing conclusions and wrong names or numbers.
A short checklist of tools and habits to use on any research task.
Write the question in one sentence, and list the key facts and words. A clear question saves hours.
Read a textbook chapter or your lecture notes to understand the area and collect leads to cases and Acts.
Look up the Constitution, the relevant Acts and cases, using Kenya Law and the library.
Confirm amendments to Acts and later cases that follow, distinguish or overrule your case.
Note full citations as you go, with page or paragraph numbers, so you never lose a source.
Use exact legal phrases in quotation marks, synonyms and the name of the Act. Try several searches, not just one.
A simple table of what you searched, where, and what you found. It stops you repeating work and helps you explain your answer.
Discuss cases with classmates to test your understanding, but write your own answers.
Law librarians know the databases and print collections well. Ask early, not the night before a deadline.
Short videos that show the skills in action. Most come from foreign teachers; the methods apply in Kenya too.
A Kenyan university lecture introducing legal research, broadcast on TV47 Kenya.
